# Draft:Battle of Mackie's Mill, Isle of Wight County, VA

Battle at Mackie's Mill, Isle of Wight County, VA
Smithfield, Virginia (January 16, 1781)
On January 16, 1781, in the wake of Benedict Arnold's devastating raid into Virginia, British regulars and Hessian Jägers clashed with local Patriot militia at a mill set along Cypress Creek just outside Smithfield in Isle of Wight County, Virginia. Though brief and small in scale, Battle at Mackie's Mill illustrated the tempo of the Tidewater expedition, the resiliency of local militia under Colonel Josiah Parker, and the tactical acumen of Hessian Captain Johann von Ewald.
I. Strategic Setting: Arnold's Tidewater Raid, Winter 1781
After defecting to the British in 1780, Benedict Arnold received a brigadier's commission and command of a mixed force of Lt Col. John Simcoe's Queen's Rangers, 80th Regiment, Loyalists of the Royal American Regiment, artillery, and a detachment of Hessian Jägers under Capt. Johann von Ewald. In early January 1781, the force sailed from New York, entered the Chesapeake, and ascended the James River with orders to cripple Virginia's war economy, seize or destroy military stores, and establish a secure base at Portsmouth. Within days, Arnold's column struck Richmond (January 5–7), inflicted heavy destruction, and then withdrew downriver, moving overland and by water toward Portsmouth, keeping detachments ready to punish militia resistance along the south side of the James.
As Arnold maneuvered through the Tidewater, he clashed with militia batteries (e.g., Hood's Point) and directed aggressive probes and landings, sometimes against Ewald's advice, to scatter local opposition and gather intelligence. The jäger diary vividly records these moments and the commander's evaluations of British decisions and American resistance.
II. Local Context: Smithfield, Cypress Creek, and Mackie's Mill
Smithfield, then a compact port town, sat on the Pagan Creek, with Cypress Creek flowing just north and west. By mid‑January, Arnold's column had debarked north of Smithfield on January 15 and encamped near town at Pierceville, while preparing to march southeast for Portsmouth. The local militia, mustering under Colonel Josiah Parker, a Smithfield native, assembled to check or harass the British as they moved. The topography of the Cypress Creek bridge and mill dams created natural choke points. One such point was Mackie's Mill, the site of the skirmish on January 16.
III. The Engagement: January 16, 1781
Forces and Intentions:
British/Hessian: Elements of Arnold's column—including Hessian Jägers (light infantry armed with rifles and short sabers) under Capt. Johann von Ewald, with detachments of British regulars/Light Infantry under command Col. John Simcoe, screened the march and pushed in militia pickets around Smithfield to keep the road net open toward Portsmouth.
Patriots: Isle of Wight militia under Col. Josiah Parker positioned at key crossings along Cypress Creek to delay, observe, and attack small detachments covering the British movement.
Action at the Mill:
Near the Mackie's Mill crossing on Cypress Creek, the militia contested the approach with cannon and small‑arms fire from cover, using the mill dam/bridge as a defensive line. The Jägers and accompanying troops executed a rapid push to turn or overrun the position, typical of Ewald's doctrine for skirmisher shock, using speed and cold steel once within range. Lt. Col. Simcoe related...
"...when the party arrived there, the enemy were in possession of the pass; and in some force; the demonstration of the cavalry and the advancing of the jagers...obliged them to retire; the bridge being taken up, prevented an immediate pursuit..."
The Patriots were dislodged after a brief, sharp exchange, withdrawing before superior discipline and numbers, while the British secured the crossing and continued the day's movement along with the arrival of Major Gordon and more British Regulars. Militia casualties included eleven dead and eight wounded militia, with nine being taken prisoner, and British casualties were three killed and five wounded.  Though casualties appear to have been limited on both sides, the skirmish achieved its operational effect: Arnold's column kept moving, unimpeded towards Portsmouth.
IV. Orientation Map:
The bridge/dam crossing at Mackie's Mill created a natural choke point on Cypress Creek north/west of Smithfield. Arnold's column camped near Smithfield on Jan. 15 (Pierceville), then pushed through on Jan. 16, meeting militia at the mill crossing before continuing toward Portsmouth.
V. Significance:
Operationally, Mackie's Mill exemplifies the hit‑and‑run geometry of the Arnold raid: British light troops brushed aside militia at tactical choke points to maintain tempo. Psychologically, such small clashes kept pressure on both local communities and British commanders. British success relied on well‑handled light infantry and jägers, but it also depended on avoiding attrition from local militias, something Ewald repeatedly flagged in his comments about risk and proper use of advanced guards.
VI. Timeline: The Road to (and from) Mackie's Mill
Dec. 31, 1780–Jan. 3, 1781 – British probe and landings along the James; artillery site at Hood's Point neutralized; Ewald records risky shore actions and his candid assessments.
Jan. 4 – Main landing at Westover (north bank of the James).
Jan. 5–7 – Raid on Richmond; destruction of public stores; withdrawal begins.
Jan. 14–15 – Arnold's force operating downriver and overland; landing north of Smithfield; camp near Smithfield at Pierceville on the 15th.
Jan. 16 – Skirmish at Mackie's Mill (Cypress Creek): British/Hessian advance elements brush aside militia under Col. Josiah Parker to keep the line of march open toward Portsmouth.
Late Jan.–Mar. 1781 – British consolidate Portsmouth as a base; continuing small actions with militia; Ewald wounded later that season near Norfolk (March 19).
VII. Assessment and Legacy:
The Skirmish at Mackie's Mill did not alter grand strategy, but it encapsulates the texture of Revolutionary War combat in Virginia in 1781: fast‑moving British columns supported by light troops and jägers; militia using terrain and infrastructure (mills, dams, bridges) to contest movement; and a contest of time—whether Virginians could delay long enough to protect resources and concentrate regular forces. Arnold's raid, including these skirmishes, succeeded tactically but arguably deepened British overextension in Virginia that culminated, after subsequent moves by Cornwallis, in the Yorktown campaign.
VII. Commemorations:
Modern commemorations in Smithfield mark January 16 as the battle's anniversary.
